label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
Dear Nana,

I’ve started this letter a few times now and kept stopping, so I’m just going to say everything properly this time.

Tomorrow is moving day. I wish more than anything that I could be sitting there in the kitchen with you and Denise instead of having her read this for me. I tried to find someone to swap the on-call week with, but it didn’t work out, and I hate that I won’t be there to help carry boxes or wrap up one last thing that suddenly turns up in a cupboard.

I know everyone has told me it’s fine, and I know you’ll tell me not to worry about it. I’m trying to listen. But I didn’t want to pretend I wasn’t disappointed, because I am. Still, I don’t want you spending your last night at the house feeling bad for me. This letter isn’t meant to make you do that. And before you ask, no, I can’t just tell the internet to behave itself for one weekend. If anything does break while Denise is reading this, though, I had nothing to do with it.

It’s hard to get my head around you leaving Kathleen Street after fifty-one years. You’ve been in that house longer than I’ve been alive. So much of what I picture when I think of you is there: the kitchen, the little television, the back steps, the smell of tea and whatever you were baking. I expect there will be a lot going through your mind tonight. I hope there’s room for the excitement, too, alongside everything else. You’re allowed to feel both.

For me, some of the best parts of being a kid happened in that kitchen during the summer. I remember the arrangement very clearly: if I dried the dishes, you’d let me stay up and watch the Expos or the Jays on that little TV. At the time, I thought I had negotiated an excellent deal. Looking back, I’m not sure my dish-drying was valuable enough to justify it, but you always held up your end. I’d be there with the game going, long past when I should have been asleep, feeling as though I was getting away with something.

I thought the important part was staying up late. Now I think the important part was that you let me sit there with you.

You also taught me crib when I was about seven, which was generous of you, and then you never once let me win, which was less generous but probably more educational. I can still remember how offended I was that you wouldn’t just accidentally miss a few points for me. You made me learn properly.

The first time I skunked you, I was fifteen, and you made me a whole pan of butter tarts. That remains one of the great moments of my life. I’ve had a few work achievements since then, and not one of them has resulted in a full pan of butter tarts, so frankly the standard was set early and everything afterwards has been a little disappointing. What I loved was that you didn’t pretend you had let it happen, and you didn’t make a big speech about it either. You just acknowledged that I’d finally got you properly. Fair and square.

I think about the back steps a lot, too. You sitting there with your tea at six in the morning, and me eventually coming out to join you. You never started talking until the cup was finished. At first I probably wanted to chatter at you, but eventually I understood that wasn’t what those mornings were for. You could just sit beside someone and let the morning happen.

My work now involves a lot of things beeping, flashing, and insisting they need attention immediately. It’s nice to remember that you taught me mornings could be quiet and that not every silence needed fixing.

You’ve always found your own way of checking that I was all right. When I got the job in Toronto, you mailed me a twenty-dollar bill taped inside a card that said, “for pizza, you look thin on the computer.” I don’t think any manager has ever assessed my wellbeing quite so efficiently.

Then last Christmas my pager went off during dinner, and you asked whether the internet was broken again and whether I’d fixed it. Now you ask me on almost every call, “Did anything break?” The honest answer, Nana, is that something is usually broken. It’s just not always the entire internet. You may actually understand my job better than most people who ask me what I do.

Underneath the teasing, what stays with me is how often you’ve made me feel welcome without making a fuss about it. Dry the dishes, sit down for the game. Finish your tea, then we’ll talk. Learn to count your own points. Here’s twenty dollars, eat something. You raised half the family in that kitchen, and somehow you still made room for each of us in ways that felt particular to us.

That’s what the house means to me. It isn’t only the rooms, although I do love them. It’s that for my whole life, it was a place where I knew how to find you. It held summers and ordinary visits and holidays and crib games and all the little routines that never seemed important enough to call traditions until now.

I know Grandpa Walt is part of those fifty-one years, too, and part of what makes leaving such a big thing. Moving doesn’t mean packing him away or leaving any of that life behind. None of it disappears because your address changes. What happened in that house belongs to you, and to all of us who got to be in it with you.

But I don’t want this to sound like some kind of final goodbye. You are eighty-eight and moving into a place you picked yourself. Nobody made you do it. You looked at what you wanted next and made the decision. I’m really proud of you for that. I imagine it takes courage to choose a new place after fifty-one years, even when you know it’s the right time and even when parts of it are exciting. I hope you know that choosing Elmwood Terrace doesn’t take anything away from Kathleen Street. It just means you’re not finished deciding what your life gets to look like.

Elmwood actually sounds pretty good. Your room is on the second floor, with a view of the parking lot and that big maple. I won’t pretend the parking lot sounds quite as appealing as your back steps, but the maple sounds promising. And you’ll be able to keep track of everyone coming and going, which may turn out to be useful information. I expect a full report on both the tree and comings and goings when I visit.

More importantly, they have a crib league. I’m not sure Elmwood fully understands what it has invited into the building. The Tuesday church ladies have had years of experience with you; these new people may wander in thinking they’re about to have a relaxed afternoon. Perhaps go easy on them for the first week. Or don’t. You never went easy on me, and I turned out mostly fine.

I like that Denise is taking the cuckoo clock and the cedar chest, and that I’ve put in my very reasonable and entirely non-negotiable claim for the crib board. Those things aren’t vanishing. They’re going to people who know where they came from and what they mean. A little bit of Kathleen Street is just spreading out around the family.

I miss the house already in some ways, but mostly I’m looking forward to seeing where you land. Elmwood doesn’t have to replace anything. It gets to be something new that is yours. You made a home for everyone else for a very long time; now you can set up this next place however suits you, at whatever pace suits you.

Now for the important business: I’m coming up for the December 5 weekend, as soon as this rotation is done. I want to see your room, inspect this famous maple for myself, and hear everything about the new place. Don’t worry if you’re still figuring out where things go. We can sit and sort through it all.

Keep the crib board handy. On that December 5 weekend, we’re having our first game at Elmwood Terrace. You can show me around, and then you can deal. And don’t even think about going easy on me—not that you ever have.

I love you, Nana. I’ll see you soon.

All my love,  
[Your name]
